unit.name: Rocks and Minerals
unit.subtitle: Identify, classify and interpret igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks and the minerals that build them

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students give a numerical age (e.g. '270 Ma') when asked to state a relative age, or fail to define what relative age means before applying it. They miss that 'relative' means older/younger than another rock unit, using cross-cutting and superposition.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Geology Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 1 Q6

common_misconceptions.topic: Sedimentary reservoirs and caps for oil, gas and water
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students apply oil-and-gas trap terminology to aquifers — calling a permeable limestone a 'reservoir rock' and a shale a 'cap rock' when discussing groundwater. They also store hazardous waste in 'reservoir rocks' for the same reason.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Geology Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 2 Q1 and Q8 (2024)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse normal, reverse and strike-slip faults — particularly identifying a normal fault as reverse, or failing to use map evidence (displacement of dyke, axial plane trace) to justify a strike-slip identification.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Geology Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 2 Q4(a)(ii); Summer 2024 Q6

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students use rock names not on the specification — gneiss, hornfels, gabbro, dolerite — when describing samples. This costs marks because the spec-listed rock is the only correct answer.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Geology Examiners' Report Summer 2025 and Summer 2024 (Component 2 Q5 and Q4)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse goniatites with ammonites or ceratites when reading suture lines. Distinguishing the three by zigzag (goniatite), wavy-but-not-fluted (ceratite) and frilled (ammonite) sutures is examined regularly.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Geology Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 2 Q5

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat porosity and permeability as synonyms, or describe a test for one when asked for the other. Desert sandstone gets recommended for hazardous waste storage because pore space is conflated with through-flow capacity.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Geology Examiners' Report Summer 2024, Component 2 Q2 and Q8

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe metamorphism as 'a bit of melting' or assume any heat or pressure will metamorphose a rock. If melting occurs, the process becomes igneous; metamorphism is solid-state recrystallisation under specific conditions.
common_misconceptions.source: Earthlearningidea: Rock Cycle Misconceptions briefing (earthlearningidea.com PDF 272)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume any layered or banded rock is sedimentary, missing foliation in schists or banding in some igneous rocks.

Students name 'convection currents in the mantle' as the sole driver of plate motion, ignoring slab pull and ridge push. The mechanism is described in the spec as 'not yet completely understood', and current science weights slab pull as dominant.
common_misconceptions.source: Mills, R. (2019). An Evidence-Based Approach to Teaching Plate Tectonics in High School. Teaching Science. ERIC EJ1220977

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cannot intuit the scale of geological time, frequently compressing it (humans coexisting with dinosaurs, or rocks 'thousands of years old' rather than millions). Linear timelines and toilet-roll analogies expose this.
common_misconceptions.source: Dodick & Orion (2003). Building an Understanding of Geological Time. SERC Carleton synthesis

common_misconceptions.misconception: When asked to describe the pattern of magnetic stripes, students give only one feature (e.g. 'they alternate') and miss that they are symmetrical about the ridge, parallel to the ridge, and alternate between normal and reverse polarity.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Geology Examiners' Report Summer 2025, Component 1 Q3(a)(ii)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students 'regurgitate' data table values without explaining differences — for example, listing that Mars lacks plate tectonics without linking this to subduction destroying Earth volcanoes and hot-spot migration limiting size.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas GCSE Geology Examiners' Report Summer 2024, Component 1 Q6(b)(iii)

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Candidates fail to tick TWO boxes when the question requires two answers. They also under-use the data sheet, sacrificing easily obtainable marks.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Calculate (Maths Skill): Candidates do not show working in the on-screen Component 1 paper, lose marks for missing or wrong units (0.1 vs 0.1 Ma; 1.97 cm/yr vs 19.7 cm/yr), and misread scale bars by failing to notice the bar is an exact fraction (1/3 or 1/5) of the feature.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Interpret Data or Diagram: Candidates measure from the wrong axis or pick the wrong period (e.g. most recent normal polarity instead of reversed) because they do not slow down to re-read the stem.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Compare Two Features: Candidates describe one feature in isolation ('Figure 2b has a fault') without contrasting against the other ('whereas Figure 2a has no fault'). Comparison questions require BOTH halves to be mentioned in each compared property.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Sequence Geological Events: Candidates describe a geological history rather than answering the question asked (e.g. 'evidence for a convergent plate boundary'). Strongest answers go earliest-to-latest, use superposition and cross-cutting, and identify the final event (e.g. small impact craters as the youngest feature on a planetary surface).
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Extended Response (QER): Polarised results: full marks or 0-2. Strong answers cite three pieces of evidence and explain each. Weak answers list evidence without explaining how it supports the conclusion, or ignore the command word 'evaluate' and concentrate only on negatives. Length is often too short for the marks allocated.

topic_weighting_notes: Component 1 is the on-screen paper (80 marks, 50%) and covers the whole specification theoretically. Component 2 is the written paper (80 marks, 50%) and is wholly based on a simplified geological map. Both papers use a data sheet.

Practical skills and techniques (Appendix B) account for at least 15% of total marks across the qualification. Component 2 in particular weights practical skills heavily — 25 of 80 marks in Summer 2025 and 35 of 80 in Summer 2024.

Mathematical skills (Appendix A) account for at least 10% of marks. Component 2 typically delivers around 17-21 maths-skill marks; Component 1 includes graph reading, scale bar measurement, standard form, percentages, half-life and rate calculations.
AO weightings: AO1 (recall) 40%, AO2 (apply) 40%, AO3 (analyse/evaluate) 20%. The 6-mark QER questions deliver most AO3 marks; multiple-choice and short structured questions carry AO1.

Rocks, minerals and fossils are reliably high-scoring across both years' reports. Plate tectonics structures, fault identification on maps, relative vs absolute dating, and extended responses on planetary geology are the lowest-scoring topic areas.

Fieldwork is a centre-level statement requirement (two field occasions, at least one directed investigation) — there is no NEA portfolio. Lessons should cover field methods conceptually (mapping, sampling, observation, compass clinometer use, graphic logs) so candidates can answer fieldwork-themed exam questions.
current_spec_changes: Specification version 2 (January 2019) amended only the 'Making entries' resit-rules section on page 23. The subject content has been stable since first teaching in 2017, first award in 2019. Reflects no content change for 2026 cohort.
Sister specification: WJEC Geology 3180QS is content-identical to Eduqas C180QS — the same plan and content will serve both boards via aliasing once Eduqas is shipped.
pedagogical_notes: EEF Improving Secondary Science (2018) recommends explicitly addressing students' prior misconceptions before introducing new science concepts. For geology, prior misconceptions about rocks, time and earthquakes are deeply embedded — surface them before teaching, then revisit at the end of each lesson.

EEF recommends modelling scientific thinking using analogies but emphasising the limits of each analogy. Examples relevant to this spec: the jelly lava-flow simulation is on the spec but candidates should know what it does NOT model (real viscosity, temperature gradients).

Dodick & Orion (2003) and SERC Carleton: deep time requires repeated exposure across multiple representations — linear timelines, ratio-based analogies (toilet roll, football pitch), and ordering exercises. A single 'age of the Earth' lesson is not enough; revisit every time the spec touches a date.

Earthlearningidea recommends teaching the rock cycle from cycle-first rather than rock-type-first to avoid the misconception that rocks follow a fixed pathway. Unit 2 lesson 4 'The Rock Cycle' sits AFTER all three rock types are introduced so it can connect the loop explicitly.

Earth Science Education Unit (UK, 2002-2015) workshops emphasised practical rock-handling for identification. Where physical samples aren't available, photomicrographs and standardised hand-specimen photographs (as used in the exam) are the next-best substitute.

Mills (2019) and Francek (2013): replace 'mantle convection drives plates' with a more accurate model emphasising slab pull and ridge push. The spec describes the mechanism as 'not yet completely understood' — content should respect that wording rather than overcommit.

Examiner-emphasised exam technique: writing answers that match the number of marks; using the data sheet; showing working in maths questions; reading the stem carefully (especially compare/evaluate command words); using only spec-listed rock names.

lessons_in_batch.title: Minerals: Properties and Identification
lessons_in_batch.description: How physical properties and acid tests are used to identify the data-sheet minerals.

lessons_in_batch.title: How Minerals Form
lessons_in_batch.description: Crystallisation routes from melt, metamorphism, evaporation, cement and hydrothermal fluids.

lessons_in_batch.title: Igneous Rocks: Texture, Mineralogy and Classification
lessons_in_batch.description: Classify peridotite, basalt, andesite and granite by colour, crystal size and mineralogy.

lessons_in_batch.title: Magma, Volcanoes and Igneous Bodies
lessons_in_batch.description: How magma viscosity controls eruption style, and how lava flows, sills, dykes and plutons are identified.

lessons_in_batch.title: Weathering, Erosion and Sediment Transport
lessons_in_batch.description: How sediment grain size, shape and sorting record transport distance and depositional energy.

lessons_in_batch.title: Sedimentary Rocks and Environments of Deposition
lessons_in_batch.description: Classify breccia, conglomerate, sandstone, shale, evaporites and limestone and read the environments they record.

lessons_in_batch.title: Metamorphic Rocks: Heat, Pressure and Texture
lessons_in_batch.description: Contact and regional metamorphism, foliation, and identifying slate, schist, marble and metaquartzite.
